summary:
**ASTRAVEN** is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring system designed to identify physiological anomalies and support early detection of potential health risks during space missions.

We developed an integrated research prototype combining machine learning, NASA-related health datasets, physiological data analysis, and an interactive monitoring dashboard. The system analyzes historical astronaut-related health observations, including metabolic, blood, and immune biomarker data, to identify unusual patterns and flag potential anomalies. It also includes a simulated real-time monitoring feature that replays physiological observations, allowing users to observe health trends and anomaly alerts through an interactive dashboard.

By combining multiple health indicators with machine learning-based anomaly detection, ASTRAVEN aims to provide a more comprehensive view of astronaut health rather than relying on isolated measurements.

This project is important because astronauts experience demanding spaceflight conditions that can affect their physiological health. Early identification of unusual health patterns could support better health monitoring, informed decision-making, and future development of intelligent astronaut healthcare systems.
details:
ASTRAVEN – AI-Powered Astronaut Health Monitoring and Physiological Anomaly Detection System

1. Project Overview

ASTRAVEN is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring research prototype designed to support the analysis of physiological patterns and health-related biomarkers during space missions. Astronauts operate in challenging environments where changes in physiological conditions can affect their health, performance, and mission readiness. Continuous observation and interpretation of health-related information are therefore important.

ASTRAVEN aims to bring multiple types of physiological and biomarker information into one integrated platform. It uses data processing, machine learning, anomaly detection, and interactive visualization to identify unusual patterns that may require further investigation.

The web application is branded as ASTROCARE – Space Health Intelligence.

2. How Does It Work?

The system follows a data-processing and monitoring pipeline:

  • Data Collection: It uses research datasets, including MMASH physiological data, complete blood count (CBC) data, and immune biomarker data.
  • Data Processing: The datasets are processed using Python-based tools to organize observations, handle relevant features, and prepare the information for analysis.
  • Machine Learning: Machine learning models analyze physiological observations and identify patterns that differ from expected patterns.
  • Anomaly Detection: Potentially unusual observations are flagged for further investigation rather than being treated as confirmed medical conditions.
  • Interactive Dashboard: Results are presented through an interactive web dashboard containing monitoring views, physiological trends, flagged observations, and model outputs.
  • Simulated Sensor Replay: Historical physiological observations can be replayed to demonstrate how a monitoring system could work in a near-real-time environment.

3. Datasets Used

The prototype integrates three main data sources:

  1. MMASH Dataset: Used to explore physiological and activity-related observations.
  2. Complete Blood Count (CBC) Dataset: Used to explore blood-related measurements and health indicators.
  3. Immune Biomarker Dataset: Used to examine immune-related biomarker information.

Combining these sources demonstrates how different categories of health-related information can be explored within one monitoring environment.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRAVEN aims to make astronaut health monitoring more organized, accessible, and data-driven.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Helping identify unusual physiological patterns for further investigation.
  • Bringing different health-related data sources into a unified monitoring platform.
  • Making complex observations easier to explore through interactive visualizations.
  • Supporting research into physiological changes and health monitoring during space missions.
  • Demonstrating how machine learning can assist in analyzing large volumes of health-related data.

The intended long-term impact is to contribute to the development of intelligent astronaut health-monitoring systems that could support mission health teams in making better-informed decisions.

5. Tools and Technologies Used

The project was developed using a combination of data science, machine learning, backend, frontend, and cloud technologies.

  • Programming Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Data Processing: Pandas and NumPy.
  • Machine Learning: Python-based machine learning and anomaly-detection techniques.
  • Backend and APIs: Python backend services and REST APIs.
  • Frontend: Interactive web-based dashboard.
  • Development and Experimentation: Google Colab and Google AI Studio.
  • Cloud Deployment: Google Cloud Run.

The prototype was developed using software-based tools and research datasets, without requiring specialized spacecraft hardware or paid external AI APIs.

6. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation of ASTRAVEN is its integrated approach to astronaut health-data exploration.

Instead of presenting physiological observations, blood measurements, and immune biomarkers as completely separate sources, the project brings them together in a common monitoring environment.

The combination of machine learning, anomaly detection, interactive visualizations, and simulated sensor replay demonstrates a practical approach to exploring how intelligent monitoring could support future space-health systems.

The project also emphasizes an accessible, modular architecture that can be expanded with additional datasets, monitoring capabilities, and real sensor integrations.

7. Factors Considered During Development

Several factors were considered while developing the prototype:

  • Availability and limitations of research datasets.
  • Data quality, consistency, and preprocessing.
  • Computational requirements for processing physiological observations.
  • Interpretability and clear presentation of anomaly-related results.
  • Accessibility through a web-based dashboard.
  • Scalability and the possibility of integrating additional data sources.
  • The importance of distinguishing potential anomalies from confirmed medical conditions.

8. Future Scope

Future development could include integration with actual wearable physiological sensors, additional astronaut-health datasets, more advanced temporal anomaly-detection models, improved explainability, and secure monitoring capabilities.

These improvements could help move the prototype towards a more comprehensive astronaut health intelligence platform.

9. Project Disclaimer

ASTRAVEN is an experimental research prototype. It uses research datasets and simulated sensor replay rather than actual live spacecraft sensor feeds. Its anomaly-detection outputs are not medical diagnoses, and the system has not been clinically validated for astronaut health monitoring. It is intended for research, demonstration, and further development.

Our Vision: To explore how artificial intelligence and data-driven monitoring can contribute to safer, smarter, and more informed human space exploration.
